papers.title: OneQuery: Unified Sequence-to-Structure Generation for Multilingual E-commerce Query Understanding
papers.authors: Mingyu Zhang, Jiejie Qin, Jianhui Ji, Rong Xiao, Meishan Zhang, Xiaoyi Zeng
papers.abstract: Multilingual e-commerce search requires robust query understanding to convert cross-lingual user queries with varied linguistic patterns into standardized semantic representations that support retrieval and ranking. However, traditional Query Understanding systems suffer from error accumulation, separately optimized subtasks that ignore their mutual correlations, and high maintenance costs. To address these issues, this paper proposes OneQuery, a unified generative framework for multilingual query understanding based on domain-specific large language models in e-commerce. We reformulate four subtasks, namely Language Recognition, Spelling Correction, Translation, and Query Tagging, into a unified Sequenceto-Structure autoregressive generation process constrained by predefined schemas, and design a three-stage progressive training pipeline with multi-task reinforcement learning alignment. OneQuery demonstrates consistent gains over baselines across all tasks and remains effective across different backbone sizes, and online experiments in the AliExpress e-commerce search scenario further confirm its practical value for industrial deployment.
papers.summary: In cross-border e-commerce search, query understanding is often split into language identification, spelling correction, translation, and tagging. Errors in an earlier stage are passed on, the stages are optimized separately, and the pipeline is expensive to maintain. Once a translation is wrong, later tagging often cannot recover. OneQuery folds those four jobs into one schema-constrained generation step, then aligns the model with a three-stage training pipeline and multi-task reinforcement learning. It stays ahead of the staged pipeline across different backbone sizes, which also suggests that domain-specific training on e-commerce queries often matters more than simply making the model larger. Generating the four subtasks together also means four separate modules no longer have to be maintained. In an online experiment on AliExpress search, the list-to-payment conversion rate rose 0.5%, and side-by-side human relevance scores rose 0.8 points, with the gains remaining stable through the trial.

papers.title: ConTra: A Training Framework for Effective Contextual Retrieval via Prefix Generation
papers.abstract: Data management systems organize large text collections for tasks such as finding relevant studies and extracting contract clauses. Systems make long documents searchable by splitting them into independently indexed chunks. Chunking can separate text from its identifying details. The indexing challenge is to keep each chunk independently searchable while preserving the context needed to find and rank it. Existing methods either encode that context in chunk vectors or attach it as a text prefix. Context encoded only in vectors is unavailable to text rerankers. Prompted prefixes serve both vector search and reranking, but are costly to generate at indexing time and can underperform contextual encoders. We propose ConTra (Context That Travels), a reinforcement learning framework for training lightweight prefix generators. Its reward combines feedback from frozen embedding and reranking models with factual verification and length control. ConTra generates one prefix per chunk during index construction and stores the augmented text and its embedding for reuse across queries. To evaluate contextual retrieval across workloads and under interference, we introduce RealContextBench, a benchmark with five application collections and three controlled conditions that isolate the effect of distracting text. On ConTEB and RealContextBench, ConTra-2B outperforms the prompted 9B baseline using Anthropic's method and the PPLX-4B contextual encoder, with a margin of up to 3.15 points over their best overall scores, while indexing short documents 7.74 times and 2.15 times as fast as those baselines, respectively. Post-trained only on ConTEB, it leads the standalone methods on RealContextBench after reranking and is less sensitive than the prompted 2B baseline to random and topically similar distractors. Code, datasets, and trained models are available at https://github.com/SStan1/ConTra.
papers.summary: To make long documents searchable, systems split them into chunks, and identifying context such as titles or clause numbers is easy to lose once a chunk leaves the source. Context stored only in vectors is invisible to a text reranker, and prompting a large model to write a prefix for every chunk is expensive at index time and not necessarily more accurate. ConTra trains a lightweight model to write a prefix that travels with the chunk, using a reward from frozen embedding and reranking models plus factual checks and a length limit. Each chunk is prefixed once at index time, and the augmented text and its embedding can be reused across queries. On two evaluation collections, the 2-billion-parameter ConTra model leads a prompted 9-billion-parameter baseline and a contextual encoder by up to 3.15 points, and it indexes short documents 7.74 times as fast as the prompted baseline. After post-training on only one collection, it still leads after reranking on another, and it is less sensitive to topically similar distractors.

papers.title: When Rerankers Work Together: Better and Faster Reranking without Joint Training
papers.authors: Yanqiao Chen, Dongsheng Hou, Yuhan Rui
papers.abstract: Standalone reranker quality does not determine its value in a multistage RAG pipeline. We systematically study heterogeneous rerankers composed without joint training, spanning lexical, single-vector, late-interaction, and joint query-context scoring. Two lightweight semantic coarse scorers, Cache-Pointwise and Cache-Shapley, learn from passage relevance labels and share cacheable representations and linear-time singleton inference. Under matched candidates and budgets, we compare cascades with stage-removal references to measure evidence retention, repair and breakage, reader accuracy, and online pruning cost. On NoLiMa 32K with Gemma, inserting these scorers before CrossEncoder or Provence improves answer accuracy by 4.02-9.43 percentage points while accelerating online pruning by 1.57-1.88x relative to the corresponding reranker alone. Cache-Pointwise composed with ColBERTv2 through reciprocal rank fusion improves accuracy by 4.60 points at 1.36x speedup over direct ColBERTv2. The stage-removal comparisons reveal an asymmetry: a cascade can outperform its final reranker alone while underperforming its coarse selector alone. Two readers, a second multi-hop dataset, and three-stage extensions show that the gains depend on the reader, reranker pairing, and stage configuration. These findings demonstrate a practical route to better and faster reranking without joint training and motivate studying stage order, candidate budgets, and rank fusion as determinants of composition quality.
company: Southern University of Science and Technology
papers.summary: In a multistage retrieval pipeline, how good a reranker is on its own does not tell you how valuable it will be in a cascade. Lexical, single-vector, late-interaction, and precise scorers can be composed without joint training. Two cacheable coarse scorers first learn from passage relevance labels, reuse representations, and run in linear time per item. The comparison holds candidates and budgets fixed, and checks what happens if a stage is removed: whether evidence is kept, repaired, or broken, how accurate the reader stays, and how much online pruning costs. On the long-context NoLiMa setting, inserting them before a CrossEncoder or Provence raises answer accuracy by 4.02 to 9.43 percentage points and speeds up online pruning by up to 1.88 times. Stage-removal comparisons also show an asymmetry: a cascade can beat its final reranker alone, yet still fall short of its coarse selector alone.

papers.title: DRBench Pro: A Knowledge-Centric Benchmark for Professional Deep Research Agents
papers.authors: Han Huang, Yuchen Yan, Xingyu Wu, Yijun Li, Chao Deng, Jie Liu, Jin Ma, Yongliang Shen
papers.abstract: Deep research agents gather information from multiple sources and synthesize it into reports on complex, open-ended questions. Existing benchmarks assess report quality along several dimensions, but lack a dedicated knowledge-centric evaluation of which research directions a report covers and how deeply it explores them. We introduce DRBench Pro, a benchmark that makes structured knowledge coverage the primary evaluation target. Our automated pipeline builds local knowledge trees from Wikipedia and uses sampled subgraphs to generate research queries and evidence-grounded rubrics. Each rubric corresponds to a relation in the tree, preserving the structure of the knowledge being evaluated. Agents receive only the research query. This structure allows us to measure breadth across major research directions and depth along related knowledge chains, with their geometric mean giving overall coverage. The benchmark includes 144 cases across 24 domains and 44,102 rubrics. Evaluating 16 deep research agents reveals different strengths in breadth and depth, with the best-performing agent reaching 57.04% overall coverage. Rubric judgments agree closely with human annotations, and agent rankings remain stable across the tested metric configurations.
papers.summary: Deep research agents gather material from many sources and write it into reports on open-ended questions. Existing evaluations often ask whether the writing looks solid, but rarely check which research directions a report covers and how deeply it explores each one. DRBench Pro makes structured knowledge coverage the main target: it builds local knowledge trees from an encyclopedia, then samples research questions and evidence-grounded rubric items, each tied to a relation in the tree. Agents receive only the research query. That setup can measure breadth across major directions and depth along related chains, with their geometric mean as overall coverage. The benchmark covers one hundred forty-four cases in twenty-four domains. Among sixteen deep research agents, the best overall coverage reaches 57.04%, and strengths in breadth and depth are not the same from one agent to another.

papers.title: Focus On Facts: Stylistically Invariant and Factually Sensitive Text Embeddings
papers.abstract: Text embedding models can conflate surface-form similarity with factual identity. Given an altered near-copy with one corrupted fact and a differently worded fact-preserving rewrite, the base model prefers the altered near-copy. We test whether hard-negative contrastive supervision can reduce this surface-similarity shortcut. We construct FOF-Bench, an 83,263-triplet benchmark spanning five domains. Each anchor is paired with an LLM-generated, fact-preserving stylistic rewrite and a matched fact-altered near-copy. We fine-tune FOF-80M (Focus On Facts), an 80M-parameter embedding model, with a triplet contrastive objective that ranks the rewrite above the factual alteration. On 8,327 held-out test triplets, the base model chooses the factually altered text in 99.58% of cases (0.42% factual preference rate; mean separation -0.1650). After fine-tuning, mean positive--negative separation is +0.0329, 98.5% of individual margins move in the intended direction, and the preference rate reaches 29.37%. On DiSC, an external style-transfer corpus, mean cross-style similarity increases from 0.7905 to 0.9559. The model also penalizes omission and transfers poorly to directional tasks such as NLI and summarization. We characterize FOF-80M as a soft factual fingerprint for studying factual retention under stylistic variation, not as a general-purpose factuality metric.
papers.summary: Text embeddings can treat similar wording as if it meant the same fact. Given an altered near-copy that corrupts one fact, and a differently worded rewrite that keeps the facts, a base model prefers the altered near-copy. The authors build a five-domain triplet benchmark so a model can learn to rank the fact-preserving rewrite above the fact-altered near-copy. On more than eight thousand held-out triplets, the base model chooses the factually altered text 99.58% of the time; after fine-tuning, that preference falls, and the rate of choosing the fact-preserving text rises from 0.42% to 29.37%. Almost all triplet margins move in the intended direction, which shows that contrastive training can weaken the shortcut from surface resemblance to factual identity, though the model is still far from judging by facts alone.

papers.title: Can Your Agent Read the Source Faithfully? Benchmarking MLLM Agents on Source-Grounded Multimodal Retrieval
papers.authors: Wentao Gao, Shizhou Huang, Junling Zhuang, Advitya Garg, Mohammad Hasibur Rahman, Mengliang Zhang, Qin Qin, Yu Yu
papers.abstract: Multimodal agents are increasingly evaluated on their ability to search the web, invoke tools, and solve complex tasks autonomously. Yet no existing benchmark systematically evaluates the capability of autonomously searching, parsing, and extracting precise answers from multimodal raw media files as a unified, end-to-end agentic task. We introduce RDQA - Raw Data Question Answering, a benchmark of 1,350 questions across three source modalities (document, video, audio), and 20 real-world task scenarios, where every answer is designed to require source access rather than model knowledge alone. RDQA provides capability-stratified evaluation through 9 capability families organized by modality and cognitive complexity, and introduces the Parametric Leakage Rate (PLR), a process-aware metric that flags correct answers produced without genuine evidence retrieval. We evaluate 12 agent systems spanning 6 backbone models and 2 scaffoldings. Our results show that the the best generic agent reaches only 24.0% adjusted accuracy, while a process-aware baseline (RDQA-Skill) reaches 41.1%. PLR reaches as high as 96.0%, indicating that many ostensibly correct answers are not grounded in retrieved evidence. We release the full dataset, evaluation framework, and a baseline to support future research.
papers.summary: Multimodal agents are increasingly asked to search the web, call tools, and finish complex tasks on their own, but few evaluations treat searching, parsing, and extracting an exact answer from raw media as one end-to-end job. RDQA covers more than a thousand questions over documents, video, and audio, and twenty real-world scenarios, and every question is designed so that the answer requires access to the source rather than parametric knowledge. Twelve agent systems were evaluated, and closed-book accuracy with tools turned off is near zero. Human overall accuracy is 57.5%, while the strongest agent configuration reaches only 24.0% after answers produced without genuine evidence are discounted. For some systems, the share of seemingly correct answers that were not grounded in retrieved evidence can reach 96.0%. Being able to search and call tools is not enough; what matters is whether the agent actually read the original source.

papers.title: Finding What Matters: Anchoring Context Knowledge with Evolving Indices for Iterative Retrieval
papers.authors: Mingyan Wu, Zhenghao Liu, Xinze Li, Yuqing Lan, Yukun Yan, Shuo Wang, Cheng Yang, Minghe Yu, Zheni Zeng, Maosong Sun
papers.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has become a dominant paradigm for mitigating hallucinations in Large Language Models (LLMs) by incorporating external knowledge. However, existing RAG systems often struggle to effectively integrate and reason over key evidence scattered across noisy retrieved documents, particularly in multi-hop scenarios. In this paper, we propose KAIR, a Knowledge Anchoring framework for Iterative Retrieval that anchors knowledge within retrieved knowledge to guide LLMs to locate the key information. During iterative retrieval, KAIR progressively updates the knowledge index to anchor salient evidence from retrieved documents. The evolving index serves as a navigational anchoring index that enables the LLM to assess knowledge sufficiency and formulate subsequent retrieval queries. Finally, KAIR generates answers by jointly leveraging the retrieved documents and the finalized anchoring index. Experiments on four multi-hop question answering benchmarks demonstrate that KAIR consistently outperforms strong RAG baselines. Further analysis shows that KAIR effectively anchors key knowledge and alleviates the context noise during iterative retrieval, improving the LLM’s ability to associate and reason over dispersed evidence across retrieved documents. All code and data are available at https://github.com/NEUIR/KAIR
company: Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications
papers.summary: In multi-hop question answering, the decisive evidence is often scattered across noisy retrieved documents, and existing RAG systems do not always gather those clues well enough to keep reasoning. KAIR updates a knowledge index during iterative retrieval, anchoring key facts and relations already seen and using them to decide what to look for next. As the index evolves, it serves as both a memory and a map, which lessens the chance that noisy documents pull the model off course. On four multi-hop benchmarks, it improves by about 20% over vanilla RAG and graph-based retrievers, and by about 10% over several deeper iterative retrieval methods. Pinning down the points already found, then choosing the next hop, is more stable than simply appending more documents round after round, and it does not require building a heavy graph over the whole collection first.

papers.title: Confidence-Based Adaptive Retrieval Fails Where It Matters Most: A Paradox in Biomedical Question Answering
papers.authors: Chengying She, Siyu Deng, Haiyan Ge, Lizhuang Liu
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for biomedical question answering, but plausible incorrect answers remain a safety risk in clinical settings. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can ground responses in medical literature, while confidence-based adaptive RAG retrieves only when the model appears uncertain. We evaluate this routing strategy on three biomedical QA benchmarks of increasing difficulty and compare models across a broad range of parameter scales. The results reveal a paradox: confidence is well calibrated (AUROC 0.78--0.89) on standard medical exam questions where retrieval adds little value (+2.4\% to -1.4\%), yet becomes \emph{near-random} (AUROC 0.506) on specialist-level questions where retrieval helps most (+11.2\%). Five uncertainty signals---first-token probability, margin, entropy, consistency-based sampling, and verbalized confidence---show the same failure pattern. Five post-hoc calibration correction strategies, including density-ratio reweighting and rank-preserving transformation, do not recover a useful routing signal on hard questions (best AUROC: 0.507). Cross-model comparison shows that larger parameter scale and higher base accuracy do not guarantee reliable confidence-based routing under specialist-domain difficulty shift. These findings challenge the premise of confidence-based adaptive RAG: in high-stakes biomedical settings, defaulting to always-retrieve is safer and more accurate than confidence-based routing when calibration on the target domain is unknown.
company: University of Chinese Academy of Sciences
papers.summary: In biomedical question answering, a plausible but wrong answer is a clinical risk. One common idea is to retrieve only when the model seems uncertain. On three biomedical benchmarks of increasing difficulty, that routing strategy produces a paradox. On standard medical exam questions, confidence is reasonably well calibrated, yet retrieval adds little; on specialist-level questions, retrieval helps the most, but confidence becomes nearly random. Five uncertainty signals show the same failure, and post-hoc calibration does not recover a useful routing signal. A larger model and a higher base accuracy do not guarantee that confidence-based routing will remain reliable when the domain gets harder. When calibration on the target domain is unknown, retrieving by default is safer and more accurate than deciding from confidence. On the specialist set, retrieval raises accuracy by 11.2%, while the ability of confidence to tell correct from incorrect answers is near chance, at 0.506.

papers.title: SPARC: Semantic Calibration with Latent Multimodal Knowledge for Robust Image-Text Retrieval
papers.authors: Zhongkuan Mao, Wenzhuo Zhao, Haidong Chen, Shangze Li, Yidong Wang, Jinhe Bi, Yunpu Ma, Junfeng Fang, Fei Shen, Tat-Seng Chua
papers.abstract: Robust image-text retrieval aims to maintain accurate cross-modal matching when image or text queries are incomplete, supporting reliable information access in real-world applications. However, existing methods typically focus on adapting to distribution shifts, without adequately addressing candidate discrimination for incomplete queries and ranking instability. To this end, we propose semantic projection and alignment with relational constraints (SPARC), which elicits latent multimodal knowledge from frozen encoders to improve candidate discrimination and ranking stability. Specifically, we first devise a semantic calibration module on a product of spheres that refines incomplete visual and textual features through tangent-space updates, maintaining the unit-sphere structure used for cosine similarity. Second, we introduce a robust semantic guidance module that combines latent multimodal knowledge encoded in complete image-text features with cross-modal semantic anchors to promote semantic alignment of the calibrated features. Finally, we introduce a matching relation constraint module that fuses original query features with their calibrated counterparts and applies a soft ranking constraint to penalize reductions in initially positive matching margins, thereby limiting ranking perturbations. Extensive experiments on Flickr30K and COCO demonstrate that SPARC outperforms competing methods under various image occlusion and word deletion settings, while achieving consistent gains across different pretrained backbones.
company: Nanjing University of Science and Technology
papers.summary: Image-text retrieval can mis-rank candidates and become unstable when a query is incomplete: a missing patch in the image, or a few deleted words in the text, can shake a match learned from complete pairs. Existing methods usually adapt to distribution shifts, and pay less attention to telling candidates apart and keeping rankings stable under incomplete queries. SPARC elicits latent multimodal knowledge from frozen encoders, calibrates incomplete image and text features on a spherical geometry, aligns them with semantic anchors from complete pairs, and folds the original and calibrated features into a matching constraint. On Flickr30K, when the center of an image is half masked, it raises average precision from 39.92% to 51.91%. When some words are deleted from the text, the gain relative to complete queries is often even larger. When queries are incomplete, the priority is to tell candidates apart, and the method does not need a separate encoder trained only on damaged queries.

papers.title: ORDER: Task-Conditioned Routing for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.authors: Aurélien Pellet, Marie Puren, Julien Perez
papers.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines typically rely on a fixed indexing and retrieval configuration determined at preprocessing time. This one-size-fits-all design is ill-suited to domain-expert settings, where heterogeneous queries require different chunking granularities, metadata constraints, and source-selection strategies. As a result, configurations that are effective for one family of queries often perform poorly for others. In this paper, we introduce ORDER (Optimal Routing for Dynamic Evidence Retrieval), a query-conditioned RAG framework that jointly adapts indexing and retrieval to the incoming query. Our approach first discovers semantic clusters over a given set of questions associated to a corpus and learns, for each cluster, a chunking strategy together with a suited metadata filtering and reranking configuration. At inference time, queries are routed to the appropriate pre-built index through nearest-centroid assignment. To further improve retrieval, we propose a supervised query router (QRe) that predicts which collections are most likely to contain relevant evidence, coupled with a Uniform Multi-source Sampler (UMS) that allocates the retrieval budget evenly across the selected sources. We evaluate our framework on large-scale, heterogeneous historical archives and show that conditioning both indexing and retrieval on the query consistently outperforms both naive baselines and strong state-of-the-art RAG systems in complex expert-domain environments.
papers.summary: Questions from domain experts often need different chunk sizes, metadata filters, and source choices, so one fixed indexing and retrieval setup can work for one family of questions and fail on another. ORDER first finds semantic clusters over questions tied to a corpus, then learns a chunking, filtering, and reranking setup for each cluster; at inference time a new question is assigned to the nearest cluster and uses that pre-built index. A supervised router also predicts which collections are most likely to hold the evidence, and the retrieval budget is shared evenly across the chosen sources. On large, heterogeneous historical archives, end-to-end answer accuracy rises from 31.0% with a naive RAG pipeline to 48.1%. Chunking and retrieval are no longer chosen independently. Choosing both the index and the retrieval path by question type keeps up better with the variety of expert questions.

scenario: Today's retrieval papers both unify cross-border e-commerce query understanding into one structured generation step, and let chunks travel with a generated context prefix. They also show that a reranker that looks strong on its own may not be the one that adds the most in a cascade. On the evaluation side, one benchmark scores deep research agents by the breadth and depth of knowledge coverage, another asks whether embeddings treat surface resemblance as factual identity, and a third checks whether multimodal agents actually read the raw source. Another line finds that model confidence can look well calibrated on ordinary exam questions, then nearly collapse on the specialist questions where retrieval helps most. Others calibrate image-text features when queries are incomplete, or choose chunking and routing by question type, instead of serving every expert question with one fixed RAG setup.
